subject: Chemistry
title: Carbon-14 Dating: Reading Atomic Clocks
description: A short lesson to help you apply Carbon-14 Dating: Reading Atomic Clocks.

hook.text: Every living thing absorbs Carbon-14 from the atmosphere. When it dies, the C-14 starts ticking away like a clock.

buildup.text: Cosmic rays hit nitrogen in the atmosphere, creating C-14. Plants absorb it as CO₂; animals eat the plants.

discovery.text: C-14 decays with a half-life of 5,730 years. Measure how much remains and you know when the organism died.

twist.text: Willard Libby invented the technique in 1949 and won the Nobel Prize. It revolutionized archaeology overnight.

climax.text: C-14 dating proved the Dead Sea Scrolls were 2,000 years old and the Shroud of Turin was medieval, not ancient.

punchline.text: Atoms decay at a known rate. Death starts the clock. Chemistry reads it.

quiz.question: What is the half-life of Carbon-14?

details.summary: Carbon-14 dating measures the ratio of radioactive carbon-14 to stable carbon-12 in organic materials to determine their age. Developed by Willard Libby in 1949, it revolutionized archaeology and geology by providing a reliable clock for specimens up to roughly 50,000 years old.
details.whyItMatters: Radiocarbon dating gave archaeologists and historians an objective timeline independent of historical records. It transformed our understanding of human prehistory and ancient civilizations.
takeaways: Living organisms maintain a constant carbon-14 to carbon-12 ratio
After death, carbon-14 decays with a half-life of 5,730 years
The method is reliable for materials up to about 50,000 years old

faq.question: Why can't carbon-14 dating measure samples older than 50,000 years?
faq.answer: After about ten half-lives, so little carbon-14 remains that it becomes indistinguishable from background radiation. For samples older than 50,000 years, scientists use other radiometric methods like potassium-argon or uranium-lead dating, which have longer half-lives.

faq.question: Has atmospheric carbon-14 always been the same level?
faq.answer: No. Variations in solar activity, volcanic eruptions, and fossil fuel burning have altered atmospheric carbon-14 over millennia. Scientists calibrate radiocarbon dates against tree-ring chronologies and coral records to correct for these fluctuations and improve accuracy.
